report.executive_summary: Heating and ventilation control packages for this public-building retrofit face one shared duty test, and all four candidates clear both qualification gates. Ranked on measured energy, P4 leads at 9 kWh, with P3 11 kWh behind, P2 24 kWh behind and P1 41 kWh behind. Inspecting the rest of the table, P4 posts the highest quality index (100) while P2 alone records a single defect. X-factors such as cost, delivery and maintenance stay unverified, so they cannot enter this ranking. However, P4 sits exactly on the five-defect ceiling, so one regrade defect would disqualify it and move the win to P3 at 20 kWh. No package is eliminated, and the strict energy rule names P4 as the client winner.
report.figure_caption: WO-02 decision flow: trusted table, qualification screen (quality at least 80, defects at most 5), energy ranking with gaps 41/24/11 kWh above the 9 kWh minimum, uniqueness audit, and open questions feeding the P4 verdict.

recommendation.rationale: All four packages qualify. P4 has the lowest measured energy, 9 kWh, 11 kWh below runner-up P3, under the strict minimize-energy policy; no cost or delivery data exists to weigh. P4's ceiling-level defect count is an audit question, not an override; if a regrade ever disqualifies it, P3 becomes the fallback on the same facts.

sections.body: The screen has two gates: quality index at least 80 and a raw defect count of at most 5. Quality runs P4 100, P3 98, P1 92 and P2 82; every value clears the floor, and P2's margin of +2 is the smallest. Defect counts run P2 1, P3 2, P1 3 and P4 5; every count is within the ceiling, and P4 sits exactly on it. Nobody is eliminated, so eligibility is settled from the table alone. All readings share one thermal load, one operating period and one acceptance basis, which makes the energy column directly comparable across all four packages.
sections.heading: Qualification screen from the trusted table

sections.body: Measured energy is P4 9 kWh, P3 20 kWh, P2 33 kWh and P1 50 kWh. Gaps above the minimum are therefore +11, +24 and +41 kWh, and consecutive rank spacing is 11, 13 and 17 kWh, so every separation is wide and the order is unambiguous on this basis. Quality spreads against the leader run 8, 18 and 2 points for P1, P2 and P3. Under the strict minimize-energy rule the ranking settles on energy alone; nothing in the supplied sources adds a weighting that could reorder it.
sections.heading: Energy ranking and gaps above the minimum

sections.body: Two candidates carry unique table records. P4 is the only quality-100 package and the only one at the five-defect ceiling; one regrade defect would disqualify it and hand the win to P3 at 20 kWh. P2 alone posts a single defect, and it also holds the smallest margin above the 80-point floor. P3 and P1 hold no unique records; P1 is last on energy (50 kWh) and unremarkable on quality (92) and defects (3). Defect exposure is therefore asymmetric across the field.
sections.heading: Uniqueness audit and defect-risk exposure

sections.body: Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability are unverified for every candidate, so no procurement or life-cycle argument can enter this decision. Four questions carry forward. First, would a defect regrade push P4 off the ceiling and move the winner to P3? Second, is P2's two-point quality margin robust to regrade, or does it fall below the 80-point floor? Third, will cost or delivery evidence arrive, and could it change a strict energy ranking? Fourth, is the shared duty basis stable across rounds, or should later work orders re-baseline the readings?
sections.heading: Open questions for the next analyst
